deep_reading.content:
Generative recommendation encodes each product as a few layers of discrete semantic IDs (SIDs), and the model generates these IDs layer by layer to perform retrieval and ranking. This Shopee paper points out one gap between it and discriminative ranking models: when a discriminative model scores a candidate it sees the product's category, shop and brand directly and crosses them with user features, while a generative model has seen no product-side information at all before it generates the first SID layer. UniRec's core technique is Chain-of-Attribute (CoA): the model first generates the product's category and then generates the SID conditioned on that category, ==which puts back into the decoding path the product features a discriminative model can use==. Alongside it come an SID construction that caps codebook load by exposure, CDC that injects scenario and combination features into decoding, and business alignment via RFT plus DPO. Offline HR@50 is 22.6% higher (relative) than the strongest baseline OneRec-V2; launched on Shopee's main feed and landing pages, orders rose 4.76% and GMV 5.60%, with 110ms end-to-end latency versus 266ms for the original multi-stage pipeline.

The paper's arXiv title is "UniRec: Bridging the Expressive Gap between Generative and Discriminative Recommendation via Chain-of-Attribute"; this write-up is based on the arXiv full text.

## 1. Where generative recommendation falls short

A discriminative ranker estimates $p(y\mid \mathbf{f},u)$, the probability that user $u$ engages ($y$) given product features $\mathbf{f}$, with all product features visible at scoring time. A generative model generates the SID layer by layer as $\prod_l p(s_l\mid s_{<l},u)$, and when generating the first layer it sees only the user, no product features.

The authors use Bayes' rule to show where the gap comes from:

$$p(y\mid\mathbf{f},u)\propto p(\mathbf{f}\mid y,u)\,p(y\mid u),\qquad p(\mathbf{f}\mid y,u)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}p(f_k\mid f_{<k},y,u)$$

$p(y\mid u)$ does not vary across products, so ranking by the discriminative score is equivalent to ranking by $p(\mathbf{f}\mid y,u)$, and the latter, expanded by the chain rule, is exactly generating product features one by one. The conclusion: if a generative model generated all of a product's features one by one, its ranking ability would equal the discriminative model's. Real systems cannot generate all features one by one because latency would be too high, so they compress product semantics into a few SID layers. Structured attributes such as category, shop and brand, which discriminative models cross directly, ==are folded into the SID during compression and no longer appear explicitly at decoding time==, and that is where the gap comes from.

## 2. Method

![UniRec overall architecture. The top part is capacity-constrained SID construction: multimodal vectors go through residual quantization over three codebooks, and clusters that exceed the load cap reassign their extra products to clusters that are not full. In the middle left is the decoder: the BOS, attribute tokens and SID tokens on the decoding side are Q, and the user behavior sequence is K and V for gated cross-attention. In the middle right is the per-step Rank Head, which concatenates the attention output, prefix embedding, content summary and aggregated representation and outputs that step's token distribution. The bottom part is alignment: the NTP loss is weighted by business value into the RFT loss, and preference pairs go through layer-wise stop-gradient to give the DPO loss.](figs/recsys26-unirec/fig1_overview.png)

### 2.1 Chain-of-Attribute: generate the category first, then the SID

CoA prepends $m$ attribute tokens $\mathbf{a}$ to the SID sequence, so generation goes attributes first, SID second:

$$p(\mathbf{s}\mid u)=p(\mathbf{a}\mid u)\cdot\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}p(s_l\mid \mathbf{a},s_{<l},u)$$

In the production configuration the attributes are the product's second- and third-level categories (categories have three levels L1, L2, L3, getting finer going down), so a product's decoding path is "L2 category → L3 category → $s_0$ → $s_1$ → $s_2$", two steps longer than before.

Why generating the category first helps: products in the same category sit close together in SID space, so once the category is known, the candidate range for the next SID layer shrinks. The authors write this as the reduction in conditional entropy $\Delta H_l=H(s_l\mid s_{<l},u)-H(s_l\mid \mathbf{a},s_{<l},u)$, which equals the conditional mutual information between the attributes and that SID layer and is greater than 0 whenever the two are correlated. With a lower error probability at each layer, the probability of getting the whole path right goes up, and beam search becomes more stable.

### 2.2 Capacity-constrained SID: balance the codebook by exposure, not product count

Existing balanced quantization (such as the RQ-KMeans used in OneRec) gives each codeword a similar number of products, but product popularity is long-tailed, and an even product count does not mean even exposure. The authors measured on Shopee production data: ranked by exposure, the top 10% of first-layer codewords take 33.24% of exposure; the top 10% of ($s_0$,$s_1$) combinations take 87.90%; the top 10% of three-layer combinations take 89.62%.

![Exposure concentration under standard RQ-KMeans. The left plot is a Lorenz curve; the closer the curve hugs the top-left corner, the more concentrated the exposure: the top 10% of sid0 codewords take 33.2% of exposure, the top 10% of sid0-1 combinations take 87.9%, and three-layer combinations take 89.62%. The right plot splits codewords by exposure rank into intervals such as 0–1% and 1–3% and counts the exposure added in each interval: the top 1% of sid0-1 and three-layer combinations alone take 49.1% and 57.3%, while 29.7% of sid0's exposure falls in the 20–50% interval.](figs/recsys26-unirec/fig2_exposure_concentration.png)

High-exposure token paths appear often in the training data, so the model keeps generating those few paths during beam search; the authors call this a Matthew effect inherited layer by layer. Capacity-constrained SID adds one constraint to the residual clustering at each layer: the sum of exposure weights $V_k$ of the products in each cluster may not exceed $\tau$ times the average load.

$$\min_{\{z_i\},\{\mu_k\}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lVert x_i-\mu_{z_i}\rVert_2^2\quad \text{s.t.}\quad V_k=\sum_{i:z_i=k}w_i\le \tau C_{cap}$$

$x_i$ is product $i$'s residual vector at the current layer, $z_i$ the cluster it is assigned to, $\mu_k$ a cluster center, $w_i$ its historical impression count, $C_{cap}$ total exposure divided by the number of clusters, and $\tau=1.05$ in production. Solving this exactly is NP-hard, so a two-step greedy procedure is used: assign each product to its nearest cluster, then move products from overloaded clusters to the nearest cluster that is not full, repeating until reconstruction error stops changing.

### 2.3 CDC: tell the model which task it is on, then add combination features

One generative model has to serve objectives such as click, purchase, add-to-cart and cross-border, and scenarios such as main feed, search, similar items and flash sale. Task-Conditioned BOS replaces the fixed start token with a learnable vector looked up by "objective × scenario", steering decoding toward that scenario's distribution from the first step.

Content Summary deals with the combined meaning of tokens: the same $s_1$ following different categories may stand for completely different products. Giving every token pair its own embedding would mean about 16 million combinations for two layers with 4,000-token vocabularies. CDC instead uses 3 hash functions ($x+y$, $x\cdot y$, $p_1x+p_2y$, with $p_1$, $p_2$ primes) to map combinations such as (L2 category, $s_0$), (L3 category, $s_1$) and ($s_0$, $s_1$) into one shared hash embedding table, concatenated into each step's combination feature $\mathbf{c}_t$.

### 2.4 Decoder and business alignment

The decoding-side sequence [BOS, attribute tokens, SID tokens] is Q; the item vectors of the user's latest 200 clicks, followed by 100 multimodal vectors fused from multi-layer SID embeddings, together form K and V, passing through 3 layers of cross-attention with a learnable gating coefficient and an MMoE-FFN. Each step has its own Rank Head, which concatenates the attention output, the embedding of the prefix generated so far, $\mathbf{c}_t$ and the aggregated user representation, and outputs that step's token distribution through SENet and MaskNet.

Next-token prediction only fits the impression distribution and does not optimize GMV directly. RFT computes a business reward for each sample, subtracts the batch mean, divides by the root mean square and clips to get $\tilde A_i$, and multiplies the sample's loss weight by $(1+\lambda\tilde A_i)$. DPO builds preference pairs from items impressed under the same request, with purchase > click > impression only, and back-propagates only through the last SID layer while the predictions of earlier layers are left unchanged, so alignment does not disturb the prefix. The two are trained together:

$$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{RFT}+\lambda_{DPO}\,\mathcal{L}_{DPO}$$

In production the RFT to DPO loss weight ratio is 20:3, and DPO's $\beta=0.1$.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Main results

This experiment is meant to show that UniRec's retrieval quality is higher than existing generative and discriminative methods. The data is 9 consecutive days of Shopee main-feed production logs, billions of interactions. HR@K generates the top K candidates with beam search and checks whether the target product is among them; "order samples" counts only samples that ended in a purchase. Baselines: SASRec, a self-attention sequential recommender that does nearest-neighbor retrieval over the SID codebook with its learned representation; TIGER, generative retrieval with an encoder-decoder architecture; OneRec-V2, decoder-only generative retrieval with cross-attention. All three generative models have 0.05B parameters.

| Method | HR@50 | HR@100 | HR@200 | Order HR@50 | Order HR@100 | Order HR@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SASRec | 0.421 | 0.489 | 0.556 | 0.548 | 0.631 | 0.709 |
| TIGER (0.05B) | 0.437 | 0.508 | 0.578 | 0.567 | 0.652 | 0.731 |
| OneRec-V2 (0.05B) | 0.438 | 0.523 | 0.587 | 0.582 | 0.671 | 0.752 |
| UniRec (0.05B) | 0.537 | 0.618 | 0.688 | 0.672 | 0.774 | 0.867 |

On all samples UniRec is 9.5 to 10.1 points above OneRec-V2; on order samples it is 9.0 to 11.5 points higher. The authors attribute the gain on order samples to Task-Conditioned BOS separating click and purchase objectives and to RFT weighting samples by GMV.

### 3.2 Which attribute chain to use

This experiment answers which category level is best to put in front of the SID. It compares no attributes against different category combinations, looking at both each step's token Top-3 hit rate and the final HR.

| Attribute chain | $s_0$@3 | $s_1$@3 | $s_2$@3 | HR@50 | HR@100 | HR@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| No attributes | 0.314 | 0.752 | 0.952 | 0.458 | 0.532 | 0.595 |
| L1 → SID | 0.488 | 0.776 | 0.961 | 0.471 | 0.569 | 0.622 |
| L2 → SID | 0.591 | 0.789 | 0.963 | 0.515 | 0.597 | 0.664 |
| L3 → SID | 0.654 | 0.801 | 0.967 | 0.517 | 0.601 | 0.670 |
| L2 → L3 → SID | 0.682 | 0.821 | 0.971 | 0.537 | 0.618 | 0.688 |

Without attributes the first SID layer's Top-3 hit rate is only 0.314; with the L2 and L3 categories added it rises to 0.682. The improvement is concentrated in the first layer ==because the first SID layer originally had no product-side condition at all==, so adding category information shrinks its choices the most. The finer the category, the higher the first-layer hit rate; generating L2 → L3 in sequence works best.

### 3.3 Component ablations

This experiment is meant to quantify the contribution of capacity-constrained SID, Task-Conditioned BOS and Content Summary; each time one component is removed and compared with the full model.

| Configuration | HR@50 | HR@100 | HR@200 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full model | 0.537 | 0.618 | 0.688 |
| SID with RQ-KMeans | 0.481 | 0.558 | 0.627 |
| w/o Task-Cond. BOS | 0.493 | 0.570 | 0.638 |
| w/o Content Summary | 0.485 | 0.565 | 0.637 |

Removing any one of the three components drops HR@50 by 4 to 6 points. After switching back to RQ-KMeans, the authors also compared the exposure concentration of the two SIDs: on three-layer combinations, the top 1% of tokens take 57.33% of exposure under RQ-KMeans and 26.04% with the capacity constraint.

![Exposure concentration of the two SID constructions; lower values mean more balanced codebook usage. The three subplots show the share of exposure taken by the top 1%, 5% and 10% of tokens, and within each subplot RQ-KMeans (red) is compared with capacity-constrained SID (blue) at the sid0, sid0-1 and sid0-1-2 levels. The two are close at the first layer and clearly apart at the second and third; for example, the top 1% of three-layer tokens drops from 57.33% to 26.04%.](figs/recsys26-unirec/fig3_matthew_effect.png)

Task-Conditioned BOS also got a multi-scenario experiment: trained on mixed samples from three production scenarios, HR@100 is 0.470 with a separate model per scenario, 0.486 for mixed training without scenario prompts, and 0.510 with the scenario BOS. Mixed training helps by itself, and adding the scenario condition improves all three cutoffs a bit more.

Increasing model width $d_{model}$ from 64 to 512 raises HR@50 from 0.397 to 0.557, without saturating.

### 3.4 Online A/B

Online experiments ran on the main feed and landing pages, with the original discriminative multi-stage recommender as control and 20% of user traffic per bucket.

| Metric | Overall | Main feed | Landing page |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orders | +4.76% | +4.27% | +5.78% |
| GMV | +5.60% | +5.42% | +6.19% |
| Page-view CTR | +5.37% | +5.37% | — |

End-to-end latency is 110ms, comparable to a single ranking model; the original multi-stage pipeline took 266ms.

## 4. Limitations

The paper has no separate limitations discussion. Two points stand out from the experimental setup. First, all offline comparisons are on Shopee's internal data, with baselines also limited to 0.05B parameters, and there are no results on public datasets. Second, the online control is the entire discriminative multi-stage system, so the A/B gain includes the combined effect of the generative architecture, CoA, capacity-constrained SID, CDC and alignment; the paper gives no per-component online contribution.

## 5. Practical implications

- If the first-layer SID hit rate of your generative retrieval is low, try CoA first: put one or two category levels in front of the SID, at the cost of only two extra decoding steps; in Table 2 the first layer's Top-3 hit rate rose from 0.314 to 0.682.
- When building SIDs, check exposure concentration, not just whether product counts are even. ==A codebook balanced by product count can still let a few popular combinations take nearly 90% of exposure==, and beam search will keep walking those few paths; adding an exposure-based capacity constraint only changes the clustering assignment step, so the cost is low.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their use as the backbone of foundation recommendation models (FRMs). Existing methods enhance recommendations through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning under a Think-then-Answer paradigm. However, explicit CoT incurs substantial inference overhead by generating lengthy reasoning traces and relies on manually designed templates that struggle to capture diverse, dynamic user interests. We propose OneLatent, an efficient latent reasoning framework that compresses explicit reasoning traces into several learnable latent tokens, enabling Latent-Reason-then-Answer inference without generating verbose traces. OneLatent first introduces Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT), which creates diverse, high-quality teacher-generated supervision by exploring user interests from multiple perspectives and automatically adapting reasoning complexity to each instance. Building on pretrained FRMs, it then uses a three-stage latent-token alignment paradigm to progressively internalize CoT traces into learnable latent tokens. Experiments on an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark show that OneLatent consistently outperforms explicit CoT-based methods and traditional baselines. Compared with the Think and No-Think variants of FRMs, OneLatent improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, while achieving over 17x higher online inference throughput. An online A/B test in Kuaishou's local-services advertising scenario shows an estimated 9.6% revenue lift over strong online baselines.

deep_reading.title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
deep_reading.content:
When a large language model serves as a recommendation foundation model, one approach is to have the model first write a natural-language reasoning trace (CoT) and then output the semantic ID (SID, an identifier that maps an item to a three-level discrete code) of the next item. The reasoning text is far longer than a three-level SID, so it holds back both decoding time and throughput; moreover, earlier work on OneReason already reported that reasoning first and then answering does not consistently beat answering directly with the same model. Kuaishou's OneLatent appends 3 fixed special tokens after the user context and trains in several steps: first the model learns to reproduce a teacher LLM's reasoning text after these 3 tokens, then it is switched to outputting the target SID directly after them; at serving time only these 3 tokens are appended and no reasoning text is generated. On Kuaishou's local-services industrial data, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.1993, 17.44% higher than OneReason-CoT in reason-then-answer mode, and its inference throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning, essentially the same as direct prediction without reasoning. ==Against the strongest baseline trained on the same teacher reasoning data and answering directly, the 3 latent tokens add only 1.58% on the industrial data, which shows that most of the gain comes from the teacher reasoning data itself==. An online A/B test on 5% of traffic estimates a 9.6% revenue lift, and the model is now serving all traffic.

## 1. Why explicit reasoning works poorly in recommendation

The input of a foundation recommendation model (FRM) is the user profile $P_u$, the chronologically ordered interaction history $H_u$ and the request-time context $\mathcal{C}_u$ (time, location, search terms and so on); the output is the SID of the next item the user interacts with. Making the model write reasoning first causes two problems. One is cost: every request must decode the whole reasoning text token by token. The other is that accuracy does not necessarily rise: an extra generation path sits between the reasoning text and the SID, and if the reasoning goes off by one step, the SID that follows goes off with it. In the paper's Table 2, OneReason-CoT in reason-first mode reaches SID@64 of 0.1697 on the industrial data, below the 0.1823 of the same checkpoint answering directly.

The authors' idea is to use the teacher's reasoning only as a training signal and keep the reasoning process in the model's internal hidden states, with no text output at inference.

## 2. Method

![The overall OneLatent pipeline (paper Figure 2). Read from left to right: the teacher model Qwen3-235B writes reasoning text from three views; the recommendation foundation model is first pretrained, then goes through three stages of latent-token alignment, and finally curriculum post-training. Note that at inference on the right, the input is only the user context plus 3 latent tokens, and the output is the SID directly.](figs/2610.30675/fig2_onelatent_framework.png)

### 2.1 What the latent tokens are

The authors add 3 special tokens $\langle L_1\rangle\langle L_2\rangle\langle L_3\rangle$ to the vocabulary, and all samples share this same set of token IDs. When the Transformer reaches these 3 positions it produces hidden states that vary with the context, and the SID tokens that follow read those hidden states through ordinary causal attention. There is no extra encoder, projection layer or decoder; the only added compute at inference is the fixed 3 tokens. The authors also state explicitly that later tokens can still see the raw context directly, so there is no guarantee that all the reasoning information is compressed into these 3 positions.

### 2.2 Teacher reasoning: three views, length adjusted to difficulty

The teacher model is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, which writes reasoning for each sample from three views:

- Exploration: given only the user profile and history, the teacher infers the user's likely consumption intents and outputs reasoning plus a list of intents.
- Evaluation: additionally told the item the user actually interacted with, the teacher judges how well that item matches the user's evidence and outputs reasoning plus a score from 1 to 5.
- Attribution: told that this item is a positive sample, the teacher explains which historical signals led to the interaction.

The evaluation and attribution views use the true item, but this information goes only to the teacher and never enters the student model's input, so the answer does not leak. The prompt also asks the teacher to first judge how complex the evidence is: samples with a clear signal converge quickly, and samples with conflicting signals get a multi-dimensional comparison. The resulting reasoning drops to 65% of its original average length (taking the non-adaptive average length as 100), and on the longest tenth of samples the semantic similarity between the two kinds of reasoning is about 0.92.

### 2.3 Three-stage alignment and post-training

The student model is initialized from Qwen3.5-0.8B and first pretrained on the recommendation domain so that SIDs and item text descriptions can generate each other:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}=-\log p_\phi(\mathcal{S}_v\mid C_v)-\log p_\phi(C_v\mid\mathcal{S}_v)$$

Here $\mathcal{S}_v$ is the three-level SID of item $v$ and $C_v$ is its text description. The latent tokens are then trained in three stages:

- Stage I: the input is "profile, history, view marker, 3 latent tokens", and the target is to reproduce one view's teacher reasoning.
- Stage II: the same input, with the target changed to all of that sample's view reasonings. The loss of each reasoning is averaged over its tokens, so that long reasoning does not take a larger share of the loss.
- Stage III: the request context is added to the input, and the target changes from reasoning text to the SID of the next item.

Post-training first runs curriculum fine-tuning from high-activity to low-activity users, then trains on a 1:1 mix of "append latent tokens, then predict the SID" and "predict the SID directly without latent tokens", so that both modes remain usable.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Main results

This experiment compares OneLatent with three groups of baselines: item-ID-based sequential recommenders (GRU4Rec, BERT4Rec, HSTU), SID-based generative recommenders (TIGER, OneRec), and reasoning-enhanced models based on OneReason. There are two datasets: 7 days of industrial logs from Kuaishou local services (test set of 20,393 instances), and Kuaishou's public LLM-Rec benchmark (test set of 10,000). The metric Hit@64 indicates whether the correct item appears among the top 64 results the model generates. The table below is taken from the paper's Table 2; NoThink and Think are the direct-answer and reason-first modes of the same checkpoint, and the parentheses give the reasoning data used for training:

| Method | Public SID@64 | Public ID@64 | Industrial SID@64 | Industrial ID@64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TIGER | 0.0078 | 0.0156 | 0.1432 | 0.0859 |
| OneRec | 0.0082 | 0.0177 | 0.1468 | 0.0900 |
| OneReason | 0.0081 | 0.0272 | 0.1658 | 0.4941 |
| OneReason-CoT NoThink (original CoT) | 0.0104 | 0.0334 | 0.1823 | 0.4936 |
| OneReason-CoT NoThink (evaluation view) | 0.0213 | 0.0623 | 0.1962 | 0.5065 |
| OneReason-CoT Think (original CoT) | 0.0089 | 0.0305 | 0.1697 | 0.4759 |
| OneReason-CoT Think (three views merged) | 0.0091 | 0.0303 | 0.1505 | 0.4567 |
| OneLatent (three views merged) | 0.0239 | 0.0742 | 0.1993 | 0.5088 |

OneLatent is highest on every metric. But the source of the gain must be read from two separate comparisons. Against Think mode, industrial SID@64 is 17.44% higher; and when trained on the same three-view data, Think mode reaches only 0.1505 while OneLatent reaches 0.1993, ==which shows that for the same reasoning data, having the model write it out token by token before answering actually lowers accuracy, because the SID is generated only after the reasoning is finished and any error in the reasoning carries over to the SID==. Against the strongest non-OneLatent result in each column, industrial SID@64 is only 1.58% higher and ID@64 only 0.45% higher; on the public data the gains are 12.21% and 19.10%. The strongest baseline on the industrial data is the model trained on evaluation-view reasoning that answers directly, and it already captures most of the gain.

On the 9B backbone, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.2008, 8.13% above the best same-size non-latent result of 0.1857 (paper Table 3).

### 3.2 Inference efficiency

This experiment checks the inference overhead of the latent tokens. The authors compare three inference modes on 872 test instances (paper Table 7):

| Method | Total time (s) | QPS |
|---|---|---|
| Direct prediction (no reasoning) | 3.17 | 274.56 |
| Explicit reasoning | 55.59 | 15.68 |
| OneLatent | 3.17 | 274.29 |

OneLatent's throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning and nearly identical to direct prediction, because each request processes only 3 extra fixed tokens and does not need to decode reasoning text token by token. The paper's conclusion says "more than 10 times", which disagrees with the 17.49 times in the body; the number in the table is used here.

### 3.3 Quality and role of the teacher reasoning

This experiment checks whether the three-view reasoning is better than the original reasoning. The authors have GPT-5.5 score 100 samples of each kind of reasoning from 1 to 5 on nine dimensions (factuality, evidence use, causal logic and so on): OneReason's original reasoning averages 3.14, the adaptive-length reasoning 3.54, and the exploration, evaluation and attribution views 4.16, 4.33 and 4.03 (paper Table 4). Training OneLatent on different reasoning data raises public SID@64 from 0.0092 with the original reasoning to 0.0239 with the three views merged, and the evaluation view alone reaches 0.0233 (paper Table 5).

As the number of latent tokens goes from 1 to 3, the hit rates of all three SID levels rise; with 4 or 5 tokens they no longer improve consistently, so 3 are used in the end.

To see what is stored in the latent tokens, the authors feed the profile, view marker and 3 latent tokens to the trained model, deliberately leaving out the interaction history, have it generate reasoning text, and compare its semantic similarity with the teacher's reasoning; the cosine similarities of the three views are between 0.79 and 0.80 (paper Table 8). The authors themselves note that the profile is still visible, so this similarity only shows an association and cannot prove that the reasoning information is all stored in the latent tokens.

### 3.4 Deployment and A/B test

![Online inference architecture (paper Figure 3). Look at the asynchronous path in the middle: new user behavior triggers a refresh, the scheduler prioritizes by user value and caps total QPS, OneLatent generates candidates asynchronously and writes them to a cache; online requests only read the cache and do not call the model synchronously.](figs/2610.30675/fig3_serving.png)

Even without reasoning text, calling the foundation model synchronously for every request still exceeds the latency and throughput budget. OneLatent is therefore deployed as a separate retrieval channel: new user behavior triggers asynchronous inference, refresh priority is set by user value and behavior strength, the generated candidates are written to Redis, and online requests take candidates from the cache, where they compete with the existing retrieval results in fine ranking. The A/B test ran in a sub-scenario of Kuaishou's local-services advertising, with 5% of traffic each for the treatment and control groups, from September 3 to 10, 2026. The treatment group's impressions rose 2.566%, ad spend rose 5.157%, and the posterior estimate of revenue rose 9.6%.

## 4. Limitations

The paper has no separate limitations section; in the body the authors acknowledge two points: the latent tokens are not a strict information bottleneck, and the reasoning information may be spread across the whole model; and the gain in Table 6 comes from the complete training pipeline and cannot be attributed to the latent tokens alone.

Two further points deserve attention. First, on the industrial data OneLatent is only 1.58% above the direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data, and the paper reports no variance across runs, so it is impossible to judge whether this gap is stable. Second, the online deployment uses an asynchronous cache, with candidates generated after the user's last behavior; the paper does not separate how much of the A/B gain comes from latent reasoning and how much from adding one more retrieval channel.

## 5. Practical implications

First, to give a recommendation model reasoning ability, the teacher's reasoning can first be used as training data rather than requiring the model to generate reasoning online. In the paper, the same three-view reasoning data reaches industrial SID@64 of 0.1993 when used as a training signal, but only 0.1505 when the model must write it out before answering.

Second, when evaluating "latent reasoning" methods, include a direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data as a baseline. On the industrial data in this paper, most of the gain already appears in that baseline, and comparing only against explicit reasoning overstates the effect of the latent tokens themselves.

deep_reading.title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
deep_reading.content:
The Netflix homepage is made of rows, each row a theme (such as "Korean TV Dramas"), with several titles laid out horizontally in each row. The old homepage was assembled by a multi-stage recommender: first retrieve candidate rows and candidate titles, rank them separately, and finally build the page. GenPage uses one decoder-only Transformer to generate the whole page directly: user history, account attributes and request information are encoded as a prompt, and ==the model generates row tokens and title tokens one by one, left to right and top to bottom==, with each row and each title taking just one token. Training copies the large-language-model recipe: first pretrain with next-token prediction on homepages that received positive feedback online, then post-train with weighted binary classification (WBC) or reinforcement learning. The roughly 200M-parameter WBC version raised the core engagement metric Netflix uses for launch decisions by 0.24% in a 14-day A/B test and cut end-to-end latency by 20%; the reinforcement learning version has not launched yet.

## 1. Why generate the whole page

In a multi-stage system, retrieval, ranking and page construction each have their own models and objectives, and feature engineering is scattered across the stages. Whole-page generation aims to solve three things. First, one model goes from raw inputs straight to a page, so fewer models need maintaining, and the problem of inconsistent objectives across stages goes away. Second, a page generated token by token can be optimized with reinforcement learning on a whole-page reward, accounting for interactions between rows: for example, when the "Continue Watching" row is at the top, users mostly resume a show they have already started and stop browsing further down; the paper calls this ability to hold attention and make users stop browsing stopping power. Third, model quality can keep improving by adding data and parameters, without repeatedly changing the system structure.

Going online brings four constraints: the homepage must be generated in real time, so latency comes first; the catalog gets new titles every day, so cold start must be handled; user interests and trends change, so the model must stay fresh; and the page must satisfy a large number of business rules.

## 2. How data becomes tokens

![Tokenization of homepage data. On the left are context tokens, equivalent to the prompt, from three kinds of data: user history (title ID, action type, action-time bucket, watch-duration bucket), account attributes (language, kids or adult account), and request information (device type, time-of-day bucket). On the right are page tokens, equivalent to the model's answer: row 1 through row N laid out in order, each row consisting of one row ID and several title IDs.](figs/recsys26-genpage/fig1_tokenization.png)

Each training example corresponds to one homepage impression and has three parts: context (user history, account attributes, request information), page (rows and titles in layout order), and feedback (plays, thumbs-up, abandonment, etc.). Only context and page are tokenized as the model's input and output; feedback is turned into a supervision signal by the reward system.

The team did not use an off-the-shelf text tokenizer but designed custom tokens for homepage data. The fact "the user watched Orange Is the New Black for 50 minutes 30 days ago" takes 16 tokens with GPT-5's tokenizer and only 4 with GenPage: title ID, action type, action-time bucket, watch-duration bucket. Each title and each row corresponds to one token, so sequences are shorter, inference is cheaper, and ==business rules can be written directly as masks on certain tokens==. The row and title vocabularies are updated daily.

The homepage is usually generated over several requests, a few rows each time. Before each page-down, the rows already generated and the user's latest actions on those rows are appended to the prompt, so the next batch of recommendations can use both long-term preferences and in-session behavior.

## 3. Reward and model

The reward comes from Netflix's existing reward system, which has been tuned through online A/B tests and aligned with users' long-term satisfaction. The system gives each impressed title on the page a scalar reward: a show binged in one night gets a high reward, a movie watched for only 10 minutes a low one, and a title the user abandons after impression a negative one. The whole-page reward is the sum of all impressed titles' rewards.

The model is a standard decoder-only Transformer with one change: input embeddings and the output projection do not share weights. Pretraining optimizes a softmax over the whole vocabulary, while WBC post-training optimizes a separate sigmoid for each token; the two need very different logit ranges, and untying the weights lets the model adapt to both objectives. The online A/B used a model of about 200M parameters, to stay within the latency budget.

## 4. Training

### 4.1 Pretraining: imitate the production system

Pretraining uses homepage impressions that received positive feedback online: given the context and the first few page tokens already generated, predict the next page token. The model is trained from scratch, not initialized from an existing large model. This step teaches the model to generate pages similar to the production system's, but it only imitates and does not directly optimize the size of the reward; after GenPage launches, repeatedly retraining on its own generated pages also risks degrading the model.

### 4.2 WBC post-training: turn generation into per-token valuation

WBC has the model estimate, given the context and the generated prefix, the value of generating each candidate row or title. Each impressed title's label is the sign of its reward (1 for positive engagement, 0 for abandonment), its weight is the absolute value of the reward, and a row's reward is aggregated from the rewards of the titles in it. Following the paper's description, the loss is written as:

$$\mathcal{L}_{WBC}=-\sum_{t}|r_t|\Big[y_t\log\sigma(z_t)+(1-y_t)\log\big(1-\sigma(z_t)\big)\Big],\qquad y_t=\mathbb{1}[r_t>0]$$

$t$ is one impressed row or title on the page, $r_t$ its reward, $z_t$ the logit the model gives this token at that position, and $\sigma$ the sigmoid. Besides each impressed target, some tokens are randomly sampled as negatives. Rarely impressed titles are drawn as random negatives far more often than they appear as positives, so the model naturally values long-tail titles lower; this acts as a popularity prior and keeps the model from ranking long-tail titles very high because of a few noisy examples.

At generation time, the model computes logits over all candidate tokens at each step, greedily picks the largest, appends it to the prefix, and generates the next. On the standard offline evaluation set for the production ranker, the WBC model beat the production ranker on title-level metrics such as weighted AUC.

### 4.3 Reinforcement learning post-training: optimize for the whole-page reward

WBC optimizes individual titles; reinforcement learning optimizes the whole page. The approach follows RLHF for large models: first train a reward model that takes any generated page and predicts its whole-page reward (the supervision target is the sum of title rewards given by the reward system), then optimize the generation policy with Dr. GRPO (a variant of GRPO that corrects an objective bias), with verl as the training framework and vLLM as the inference engine. The policy, reference model and reward model are all initialized from the pretrained checkpoint. The reward model's training data comes from the production policy and is only reliable on pages similar to production ones, so the policy is kept near the reference model with a KL penalty, to stop the policy from generating pages the reward model would wrongly score high. There are also rule-based rewards, for example that the page must have a row-by-row structure and that business-critical rows must not be placed too far down.

## 5. Engineering problems to solve for launch

Cold start has two remedies. One is to write the metadata of new titles or time-sensitive content such as live events directly into the context tokens. The other is semantic embedding fusion: each title's input embedding fuses an ID embedding with a content embedding built from the synopsis, cast, subtitles, genre and video content, so a new title has a usable representation even with few interactions.

Freshness relies on multi-cadence incremental training: every so often, a full pretraining and post-training pass over a longer history window; between those passes, post-training continues daily from the previous day's checkpoint on the most recent day of data plus a sample of historical data, keeping up with new titles and trends without forgetting old knowledge. New rows and new titles are first initialized with the fallback token of their type, and during training a small fraction of known tokens is randomly replaced with fallback tokens, so the model learns to handle tokens it has never seen.

Business rules are guaranteed by constrained decoding: at each step a mask of allowed tokens is computed from the applicable rules and multiplied onto the output logits, so only compliant tokens can be generated. For example, to pin the "Popular Games" row to row 2, all other row tokens are masked at the row-2 position. Rules vary by request, so the masks must be built dynamically per request and per position, and the team modified the inference engine for this.

Each row autoregressively generates only its first few titles, because those draw the most attention and most determine the impression the row makes; the remaining positions are filled with one forward pass conditioned on that prefix, taking the highest-logit compliant titles. This is called hybrid row decoding and is used to reduce decoding steps.

## 6. Experiments

### 6.1 Does pretraining help

This experiment is meant to show that pretraining gives WBC post-training a better starting point. It compares pretraining followed by WBC against doing WBC directly.

| Metric | With pretraining | Without pretraining |
|---|---|---|
| Loss (weighted BCE) | 0.321 | 0.333 |
| Row AUC | 0.884 | 0.879 |
| Entity AUC | 0.920 | 0.910 |

Entity AUC going from 0.91 to 0.92 looks small, so the authors restate it: ignoring example weights, if you randomly draw a pair of impressed titles (one positive, one negative), the probability the model orders them wrongly drops from 9% to 8%. On a mature production system, a single change rarely brings an improvement this large.

### 6.2 Add parameters or add context

This experiment compares the gains from two ways of improving: scaling the model from about 120M to 900M parameters, versus keeping the model size fixed and progressively enriching the prompt's content and tokenization.

![The left plot shows pretraining loss (cyan, left axis) and WBC post-training loss (red, right axis) as model parameters go from 120M to 900M; both fall roughly as a power law in parameter count, with WBC loss dropping from about 0.3265 to about 0.3222. The right plot fixes model size and progressively enriches the context, with WBC loss normalized to 1.0 at step 1, falling to about 0.93 after 6 steps.](figs/recsys26-genpage/fig3_4_model_vs_context.png)

Scaling the model about 7.5x lowers WBC loss by only about 1.3%; enriching the context lowers it by about 6.9% cumulatively, and several single context improvements each gained more than the whole parameter scale-up. The authors' judgment is that ==at the current stage, personalization quality is limited first by the information available to the model and how it is represented, and only then by capacity==. The two experiments use different axes, and each context step is measured as an improvement over the previous step on a different data snapshot and then multiplied together, so only relative comparisons are possible.

### 6.3 Is reinforcement learning optimizing the whole page

This experiment is meant to show that reinforcement learning learns a page-level policy rather than greedy token-by-token choices. The reward rises steadily during training, but it is computed by the same reward model the policy is optimizing, so it only counts as a sanity check. More convincing is diversity: measured by pairwise embedding distance between titles on the page, it is not part of the training objective, yet it also rises during training.

![Reinforcement learning post-training curves, with reward (red) and diversity (cyan) both normalized to 1.0 at the pretrained checkpoint. Within 140 steps the reward rises to about 1.54 and diversity to about 1.15 to 1.17, even though diversity is not part of the training objective.](figs/recsys26-genpage/fig5_rl_diversity.png)

### 6.4 Online A/B

The online control is the existing multi-stage homepage recommender, and the treatment is the roughly 200M-parameter WBC model. To keep business rules such as eligibility checks, GenPage decodes within the candidate row and title sets produced by the existing system. There are 5 treatment arms, differing in the number of random negatives and which online impressions are included in training.

| Result | Value |
|---|---|
| Core engagement metric (5 treatment arms) | All significantly up, p<0.001 |
| Best treatment arm | +0.24%, 95% confidence interval [0.17%, 0.30%] |
| End-to-end latency | -20% |

The 5 configurations gained similar amounts, showing that the gain does not depend on one particular training-data setup. The authors call it one of the largest algorithm-driven gains in recent years. Latency dropped because one Transformer consumes tokenized raw inputs directly, replacing several ranking stages and a lot of feature computation, while custom tokens and hybrid row decoding reduce decoding steps, and the available optimizations are not yet exhausted.

Two more things were observed after launch. First, the latest in-session actions quickly influence later recommendations and fall back to long-term preferences after a day or two, showing the model really uses action timestamps, which the old system needed many hand-crafted features to do. Second, the composition of impressed content changed unexpectedly: for example, the ratios of new to old titles, series to movies, and high-quality to low-quality engagement all shifted. The authors speculate this is because GenPage's personalization is more precise, exposing that components inherited from the old system, such as the reward system, are not yet aligned with the generative paradigm, and they will tune these components next.

## 7. Limitations

The authors list three unfinished parts: reinforcement learning post-training has not launched; long context still relies on hand-designed summaries; and text, multimodal and reasoning capabilities have not been brought in. Reinforcement learning also has two open problems: offline evaluation depends on the reward model the policy is optimizing, so the conclusions are circular; and WBC decomposes fully by title while whole-page reinforcement learning does not decompose at all, and how to exploit partial structure between the two remains unanswered.

In addition, the online experiment decodes within the candidate sets from the old system and does not replace the retrieval stage, so this A/B validates ranking and page construction, not fully end-to-end generation.

## 8. Practical implications

- If you work on generative recommendation, check your tokenization first: one item or one layout unit per token keeps sequences short, and business rules can be written directly as logit masks, without maintaining complex constraints over a multi-token text vocabulary.
- Enrich the context before scaling the model. In Netflix's data, the cumulative loss reduction from context improvements is about 5 times that from a 7.5x parameter scale-up.

papers.summary: Because attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, generative recommenders usually consume only short behavior sequences. papers.abstract: Generative recommendation is a coarse-to-fine process in which Semantic ID prefixes determine broad categories and suffixes identify items. GLASS injects distinct long-term user signals into these stages through SID-Tier for prefix generation and semantic hard search with gated fusion for suffix generation. Experiments on TAOBAO-MM and KuaiRec outperform prior baselines, and a two-week online A/B test on a short-video platform reports significant recommendation-quality gains.

deep_reading.content:
Generative recommendation encodes each item as a few levels of semantic IDs (SIDs) and uses a Transformer to generate the next item one code at a time. Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so these models usually take only the most recent few dozen behaviors. In the paper's two datasets, the average user history length is 987 (TAOBAO-MM) and 884 (KuaiRec), yet the model input keeps only the last 50. The authors also observe a pattern: in plain generative retrieval, after the first-level code is generated, the true item's rank in the beam gets worse rather than better, with the average rank dropping by 1.25 at the second level. GLASS ==uses the long-term history differently for each SID level==: before generating the first-level code, it compresses the whole long-term history into one interest token fed to the encoder; after the first-level code is generated, it uses that code as a retrieval key to pull items of the same broad category from the long-term history, which help generate the last two codes. On TAOBAO-MM, R@1 is 21.57% higher than the strongest baseline, DualGR; in a two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, app usage time per user rose 0.052% and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

## 1. The problem: getting long histories into generative retrieval

The ranking stage has a mature recipe for long sequences, SIM's two-stage design: a GSU (General Search Unit) first uses the target item to retrieve a relevant sub-sequence from the long history, then an ESU (Exact Search Unit) runs fine-grained target attention over it. The retrieval stage has no target item, so the GSU has nothing to search with. OneRec and OneSearch use a Q-Former to compress long-term behavior into fixed-length vectors, which stops at the granularity of interest clusters. DualGR already uses SIDs as retrieval keys in generative retrieval, but it treats codes at every level the same way.

The authors start from the structure of SIDs themselves. The first-level code decides which broad category an item belongs to, and the last two codes locate the specific item inside that category. When the first-level code is generated there is no path yet, so the model needs the user's overall preference across categories; when the last two codes are generated the category is fixed, so the model needs what the user actually engaged with inside that category. ==The two levels need long-term information at different granularity, so it is injected in two places==.

## 2. Overall structure

![The three parts of GLASS. On the left, (a) is the encoder-decoder backbone: the short-term sequence goes through a lookup table and self-attention into the encoder, and the SID-Tier at the bottom right outputs one token appended after the short-term sequence; each decoder layer has two cross-attention paths, one over the encoder output and one over the long-term items returned by Semantic Search, and the Gate in the middle merges them with weights g and 1−g. Top right, (b) is SID-Tier: similarity is computed between each first-level code and every item in the long-term history, counted into a histogram by similarity bin, normalized, and passed through an MLP. Bottom right, (c) is semantic search: the generated first-level code <a_5> hard-matches items in the long-term history whose first-level code is the same (Item1, Item3), and neighboring codes <a_2> and <a_8> are added when there are too few.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig1.jpg)

The backbone is a TIGER-style encoder-decoder. Each item's multimodal vector is quantized by RQ-VAE into three levels of codes; on the public datasets the codebook sizes are [64,128,128], the embedding dimension is 96, and the encoder and decoder each have 4 layers. The user history is sorted by time and split in two: the most recent 50 behaviors are the short-term sequence, and everything earlier is the long-term sequence.

## 3. First-level code: SID-Tier compresses the long-term history into one token

This step addresses the fact that the first-level code is generated with no clue at all. Running attention directly over the long-term history is too expensive, so the authors exploit the small size of the first-level codebook: there are only tens to a little over a hundred first-level codes, so cross features between the user history and every code can all be computed.

Each first-level code $k$ first gets a prototype vector $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_k$, the mean of the vectors of all items whose first-level code is $k$. The cosine-similarity range $[-1,1]$ is then split evenly into $N$ bins, and for each first-level code the model counts how many long-term history items fall into each bin:

$$\mathbf{t}_k[j]=\sum_{v\in H^{id}_{long}}\mathbb{I}\big(\text{bin}(\text{Cos}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_k,\mathbf{h}_v))=j\big)$$

$\mathbf{h}_v$ is the multimodal vector of history item $v$, $\text{bin}(\cdot)$ maps a similarity to its bin, and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function. Intuitively, $\mathbf{t}_k$ describes how many items in the user's history are very similar to category $k$, how many are somewhat similar, and how many are not. The histograms of all first-level codes are concatenated into a vector of length $K_0\cdot N$, compressed by an MLP (hidden size 256) into one $d$-dimensional vector $\mathbf{e}_{tier}$, and appended after the short-term sequence embedding before entering the encoder.

This token depends only on the user history and the codebook, not on the item being generated, so it can be precomputed offline. It is really the familiar "user's historical preference statistics per category" feature from ranking models, computed over first-level SID codes instead.

## 4. The last two codes: retrieve from the long-term history with the generated first-level code

After the first-level code $\hat{c}_0$ is generated, the model takes every item in the long-term history with the same first-level code:

$$H_{ret}=\{c(v_i)\mid v_i\in H^{id}_{long},\ c_0(v_i)=\hat{c}_0(v_{n+1})\}$$

This is SIM's hard search with the key changed from "the target item's category" to "the first-level code just generated". Each decoder layer runs self-attention and then two cross-attention paths in parallel: one with the encoder output as key/value, giving $\mathbf{Z}_{short}$; one with the retrieved item embeddings as key/value, giving $\mathbf{Z}_{ret}$. A gate merges the two:

$$\mathbf{g}=\sigma([\mathbf{Z}_{short};\mathbf{Z}_{ret}]\mathbf{W}_g),\qquad \mathbf{Z}_{context}=(\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{g})\odot\mathbf{Z}_{short}+\mathbf{g}\odot\mathbf{Z}_{ret}$$

$\mathbf{W}_g$ is a $2d\times d$ projection and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. A large $\mathbf{g}$ tilts the result toward the retrieved long-term items; a small $\mathbf{g}$ tilts it toward the short-term sequence. The training objective is the standard autoregressive cross-entropy over the three codes.

## 5. What if too few items come back

Hard search has an obvious problem. In the paper's example, with a history of 1000 and a first-level codebook of 128, each first-level code retrieves only about 7.8 items on average: too little information, with a high share of noise. The authors offer two fixes:

- **Semantic neighbor augmentation**: precompute cosine similarities between first-level codes and record each code's top-k nearest neighbors. When fewer items than a threshold $\tau$ come back, the history items under the neighbor codes are merged in as well.
- **Shrinking the first-level codebook**: make the first-level codebook smaller during training so that each first-level code covers more items. The first level is responsible for volume, the last two for precision.

**Main results**. The goal is to show that GLASS beats both ID-based sequential models and SID-based generative models. Both datasets keep only positive feedback: TAOBAO-MM keeps clicks, uniformly samples 10,000 items and keeps those that appear at least 5 times in the training set; KuaiRec keeps samples whose play time exceeds the video length. The authors define Conditional Rank Progression (CRP): over samples whose first $d-1$ codes all stayed in the beam, the average rank of the correct level-$d$ code among the top-K candidates; closer to 1 is better. The paper has no separate limitations discussion; two facts are worth keeping in mind. The public datasets are small: KuaiRec has only 3790 users and TAOBAO-MM's items are sampled down to 10,000, far from industrial codebook scale. - Append the "user's historical preference histogram over first-level codes" as an extra token to the encoder input; it can be computed offline and adds almost no online cost.
- Before doing hard search with the generated first-level code, measure how many items each first-level code retrieves from user histories on average; if too few, try shrinking the first-level codebook first and neighbor augmentation second.

The ranking stage has a mature recipe for long sequences, SIM's two-stage design: a GSU (General Search Unit) first uses the target item to retrieve a relevant sub-sequence from the long history, then an ESU (Exact Search Unit) runs fine-grained target attention over it. The retrieval stage has no target item, so the GSU has nothing to search with. OneRec and OneSearch use a Q-Former to compress long-term behavior into fixed-length vectors, which stops at the granularity of interest clusters. DualGR already uses SIDs as retrieval keys in generative retrieval, but it treats codes at every level the same way.

The authors start from the structure of SIDs themselves. The first-level code decides which broad category an item belongs to, and the last two codes locate the specific item inside that category. When the first-level code is generated there is no path yet, so the model needs the user's overall preference across categories; when the last two codes are generated the category is fixed, so the model needs what the user actually engaged with inside that category. The two levels need long-term information at different granularity, so it is injected in two places.

The backbone is a TIGER-style encoder-decoder. Each item's multimodal vector is quantized by RQ-VAE into three levels of codes; on the public datasets the codebook sizes are [64,128,128], the embedding dimension is 96, and the encoder and decoder each have 4 layers. The user history is sorted by time and split in two: the most recent 50 behaviors are the short-term sequence, and everything earlier is the long-term sequence.

This step addresses the fact that the first-level code is generated with no clue at all. hv​ is the multimodal vector of history item v, bin(⋅) maps a similarity to its bin, and I is the indicator function. Intuitively, tk​ describes how many items in the user's history are very similar to category k, how many are somewhat similar, and how many are not. The histograms of all first-level codes are concatenated into a vector of length K0​⋅N, compressed by an MLP (hidden size 256) into one d-dimensional vector etier​, and appended after the short-term sequence embedding before entering the encoder.

This token depends only on the user history and the codebook, not on the item being generated, so it can be precomputed offline. It is really the familiar "user's historical preference statistics per category" feature from ranking models, computed over first-level SID codes instead.

papers.title: CSG4Rec: Collaborative-Similarity Guided Semantic IDs Tokenization for Generative Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Wei Liu, Bo Yang, Qianyang Zhu, Ruijie Xiao, Sirui Huang, Qing Li
papers.summary: The semantic IDs used in generative sequential recommendation are usually produced by quantizing item text embeddings layer by layer, so items with similar text get similar codes; collaborative information such as "often bought by the same users" never enters the codes. CSG4Rec adds a contrastive loss when training the tokenizer: the quantized vectors of two items with similar collaborative behavior are pulled together and those of dissimilar items are pushed apart, ==so that items with similar codes are similar in both text and user behavior==. It also aggregates the embeddings of each user's historically interacted items and quantizes them into a user semantic ID, which is fed into the generative model together with the item semantic IDs. The authors report gains over existing baselines on three benchmark datasets.
papers.abstract: The paper proposes collaborative-similarity guided semantic-ID tokenization that fuses semantic and collaborative information in one space. It also constructs user semantic IDs to capture preference characteristics and builds CSG4Rec for generative sequential recommendation. The method is designed to address the mismatch between content-derived identifiers and collaborative behavior signals.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-based conversational recommenders with semantic and genre-aware metrics
papers.authors: Darshna Parmar, Dhruv Shah, Pramit Mazumdar, Saurav Mallik
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, Recall@K and BLEU count an LLM's movie suggestion as wrong whenever it is not the exact labeled answer, even if both are action comedies. The authors find that the labeled answer appears in the top 10 recommendations only 39% of the time, while another 53% of recommendations share at least a genre with the answer. They build one unified pipeline: a prompt extracts titles, genres and actors from the user's words, these are used to filter candidate movies from a knowledge graph, and an LLM generates the reply; six instruction-tuned models are compared on two movie dialogue datasets, ReDial and INSPIRED. Two new metrics, GHR@10 and SoftGHR@10, score whether the top 10 recommendations overlap the answer in genre, with SoftGHR also crediting partial overlap. The authors conclude that ==recommendation quality and fabrication depend on the knowledge graph and dialogue context, not on model size==.
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems powered by large language models generate fluent dialogue but remain difficult to evaluate with lexical metrics. This study benchmarks systems on ReDial and INSPIRED using a pipeline that combines natural-language understanding, dialogue management, knowledge-graph reasoning and LLM generation. It introduces genre-aware measures for preference alignment and analyzes how model size, knowledge grounding and context affect quality and hallucination.

papers.title: Integrating implicit desire fusion for proactive conversational recommendation systems with LLMs
papers.authors: Sitong Yan, Shengli Song, Chengen Lai, Jingyang Li, Guangneng Hu
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, users often cannot say what they want, and asking about attributes turn after turn drags the dialogue out. DESIRE trains no model; it uses LLMs such as GPT-3.5-Turbo with prompts to handle each turn: it first summarizes the dialogue context, the user's historical preferences, attributes retrieved from the item database and this turn's accept or reject feedback into a needs description, then decides whether to keep asking or to recommend; when asking it picks one of five question types, when recommending it picks one of six persuasion strategies such as presenting evidence or social proof, and item attributes in the reply may only come from retrieval results. Evaluation uses an LLM-simulated user. On LastFM the success rate within 15 turns (SR@15) is 0.583, versus 0.544 for the multi-agent baseline MACRS; removing the needs-summary step drops it to 0.327, ==showing that the success rate mainly comes from summarizing multiple signals first and then deciding whether to ask or recommend==.
papers.abstract: The paper introduces DESIRE, a desire-oriented conversational recommendation framework combining implicit desire exploration with recommendation strategy planning. It targets precision, proactivity and persuasion in user-centric dialogue. Evaluation on LastFM and Yelp reports improved recommendation quality and dialogue persuasiveness in music and e-commerce scenarios.
